excerpt: How to find a free course that is worth your data, judge a teacher in five minutes, take notes that stay useful, and avoid the courses that sell nothing.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to learn online without paying for courses you do not need. You will find free material, judge whether a teacher is worth your time, take notes you can use, and finish something rather than starting five things.
Most of what a beginner needs is already free. The difficulty is not access but choosing, and the choice is easier with three simple tests.
Before you start

items: A connection you can afford for an hour or two a week.
A notebook, paper or digital.
A subject you actually need, not one that merely sounds impressive.

body.text: Where free teaching lives

items: Video sites carry a tutorial for almost any task, often with the steps written below.
Khan Academy covers school and early college maths and science without charge.
freeCodeCamp teaches programming with exercises you do in the browser.
Many universities publish their lecture recordings and reading lists openly.
Your bank, your network provider, and some government offices publish free guides.
Public libraries often lend ebooks and give access to learning platforms.

body.text: You will see the search results offer hundreds of options for any subject, which is the first problem. Choose one course and finish it before opening a second.

body.alt: A laptop playing a tutorial video with a notebook beside it.
body.caption: One video, one notebook. Writing the steps down is what turns watching into knowing.

body.text: It looks like the longest course must be the most complete. A four-hour course that you abandon teaches less than a forty-minute one you finish.
Judge a teacher in five minutes

items: Watch the first two minutes and check that the sound is clear.
Check whether the steps appear on screen or only in speech.
Look at the upload date, since menus and prices change.
Read three recent comments, which usually mention errors or missing steps.
Check that the teacher names the version of the software being used.
Leave if the first two minutes are an advertisement for a paid course.

body.text: A good tutorial will show the screen as it teaches, at a size you can read, and say the steps in order. If you cannot follow the screen, no amount of listening will fix it.

body.alt: A phone showing lesson notes typed in a notes app.
body.caption: Notes in your own words, with the date. A month later those notes are the lesson, and the video is gone.

body.text: Take notes that work later

items: Write the steps as commands, not as sentences, so you can follow them again.
Note the exact menu names, since those are what you will search for.
Write one question beside each section you did not understand.
Do the actions on your own machine while the video plays.
Pause and repeat the awkward section rather than letting it pass.
End the session with one sentence: what can I now do that I could not before.

body.text: None of this needs a paid app. A text file with headings for each topic is enough, and it is searchable in a way that paper is not.
Do not worry about the pace. Two hours a week for three months beats a weekend of enthusiasm that ends on Sunday night.
Avoid the courses that sell nothing

items: Be careful with any course that promises a salary in a fixed number of weeks.
Decline anything that asks for a payment before you see a lesson outline.
Check whether the platform is known, rather than trusting one advert.
Avoid a course that requires you to recruit others, which is not teaching.
Check the refund terms before paying for anything, even a small amount.
Prefer a course with a certificate from an institution you can name.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a correction, and none of them costs you the whole effort.

items: You started five courses and finished none: choose one and hide the rest for a month.
You cannot follow the accent: turn on captions and slow the video down.
The software looks different: search for a newer tutorial, or read the current menu names.
The notes make no sense later: rewrite one page the same evening, while it is fresh.
You paid for a course you cannot use: ask for a refund within the platform's window.
You feel too old to start: the first lesson does not know your age, and it works the same.

body.text: Practice
One subject, one course, one page of notes this week.

items: Write down one thing you need to learn for work or business.
Find three free options and compare their first two minutes.
Choose one and note its length.
Do the first lesson with a notebook open.
Write the steps in your own words before you close the laptop.

body.text: You can now learn without waiting for a classroom. In the next lesson you will build the profile that employers actually read.

excerpt: Building a work profile that survives a ten-second scan, uploading a CV that opens, and applying without paying anybody for a job.

body.text: This lesson builds a work profile on a job site and a CV that survives the upload. You will write a headline, describe your experience plainly, upload a file that opens, and apply without paying anybody for a job.
A recruiter looks at a profile for about ten seconds before deciding. Those ten seconds are spent on the photo, the headline, and the first line of the summary, which is where the effort belongs.
Before you start

items: Your one-page CV as a PDF.
A clear photograph of your face, in daylight.
An email address that uses your name.
About an hour.

body.text: The parts that matter first

items: Photo: shoulders and face, plain background, taken in daylight.
Headline: the job you want, in the words the job advert uses.
Location: your city or area, since many employers filter by it.
Summary: three sentences on what you do and what you have done.
Experience: job title, employer, dates, and two or three results.
Skills: the tools and tasks named in the adverts you are targeting.

body.text: You will see the profile preview update as you type, with each section appearing as a block on a page. Check the preview at phone size, since most recruiters first see it there.

body.alt: A laptop showing a professional work profile being filled in.
body.caption: The headline and the first three lines carry the whole profile. Everything below is read only if those work.

body.text: It looks like a longer profile looks more serious. Length is not the problem; vagueness is, and three specific lines beat three paragraphs of description.
Write experience as results

items: Start with the job title and the employer, then the dates.
Describe what you did with numbers where they exist.
For example: handled forty customer calls a day, or managed stock worth two million naira.
Use the same words as the advert, since many systems search for them.
Include unpaid work that proves a skill, such as managing a family shop.
Leave out anything you cannot explain if asked in an interview.

body.text: None of this needs a paid profile upgrade. The free version carries the photo, the summary, the experience, and the file, which is everything an employer reads.
The uploaded file will appear as a small line under the button, with the file name and a tick. If that line shows a photograph icon instead of a page, the CV went up as an image.

body.alt: A job portal with a CV upload field and a selected PDF file.
body.caption: Upload the PDF, not a photograph of the CV. A phone photo of paper often fails to open on the employer's system.

body.text: The file that must open

items: Save the CV as a PDF, which keeps the layout on any computer.
Name the file with your name, such as cv-chinedu-okafor.
Keep it to one page, or two if you have more than eight years of work.
Check the file opens on a phone before uploading it.
Check the fonts did not change, which happens when a document is exported badly.
Keep the original document, so you can edit and export again.

body.text: Do not worry about not having a long work history. A short, honest CV that opens correctly is better than a long one that arrives blank.
Apply without paying

items: Apply through the employer's own page or a known job site.
Never pay a fee for a job, an interview, or training before a start date.
Check the employer's address and phone number on their own website.
Read the advert again before applying, and match your headline to it.
Keep a list of jobs applied for, with dates, so you can follow up.
Send a short message after a week if the advert names a contact.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a repair, and the first is the most common.

items: The employer cannot open your CV: upload the PDF rather than a photo or a document file.
No replies after twenty applications: the headline is vague. Rewrite it for each advert.
The photo looks unprofessional: retake it in daylight against a plain wall.
Your profile shows an old job as current: edit the dates, since recruiters check.
A recruiter asks for a fee: refuse, and report the advert to the site.
The file name looks careless: rename it before uploading, which takes ten seconds.

body.text: Practice
Improve one section properly rather than all five badly.

items: Rewrite the headline using one real job advert.
Take a new photo in daylight against a plain wall.
Add numbers to two lines of experience.
Export the CV as a PDF and open it on a phone.
Apply for one job and note the date.

body.text: You can now be found by the people who are hiring. In the next lesson you will handle a call from a voice that sounds like family and is not.

excerpt: How a recorded voice can be copied, the question that breaks the illusion, and what to do in the first hour if money has already gone.

body.text: This lesson is about calls and voice notes that sound like a relative in trouble. You will learn how a voice gets copied, the one question that ends the pretence, and what to do if money has already left.

A short recording from social media is enough for software to copy a voice. The call then sounds like somebody you know, which is why a rule agreed in advance matters more than suspicion in the moment.
Before you start

items: A family member to talk to, today.
Ten minutes.
A pen, to write one agreed question.

body.text: How the call works

items: The caller uses a voice that sounds like your child, brother, or colleague.
The story involves an accident, an arrest, or a hospital, always urgent.
There is a reason they cannot talk for long, or cannot come to the phone.
The money must go to a different name, often a driver or a police officer.
The caller asks you to keep it quiet, which prevents a second opinion.
The number is unknown, or a message app instead of a normal call.

body.text: You will see a message from an unknown number, or a call from a name that does not match the voice. That mismatch is the first sign, and it is hard to notice while you are frightened.

body.alt: A phone showing an incoming call from an unknown number.
body.caption: A familiar voice from an unknown number is a contradiction. Stop, and check it before you do anything else.

body.text: It looks like recognising a voice is proof of who is calling. A copied voice has no memories, and one personal question exposes it in seconds.
The question that ends it
Agree a family question whose answer is not on the internet. Then ask it, and listen for the pause.

items: Ask something only that person would know, such as a childhood nickname.
Ask about a recent event that was never posted online.
Ask them to call back on their own number, which takes a minute.
Ask a question with a false premise, such as the name of a pet they never had.
Hang up and call the person directly on the number saved in your phone.
Message another family member and ask whether the story is true.

body.text: A real relative will answer the question and may be annoyed. A copied voice will stall, change the subject, or produce an answer that is almost right, which is the giveaway.

body.alt: A family group listening to a phone call on speaker.
body.caption: Put the call on speaker and let somebody else listen. A second pair of ears hears the odd details.

body.text: If money has already gone

items: Call your bank immediately and report the transfer as a fraud.
Give the bank the time, the amount, and the account it went to.
Report to the police and get a written report with a reference number.
Tell the person whose voice was copied, so they can warn their contacts.
Keep every message and call record, since those are the evidence.
Change the passwords on the accounts that hold the contact list.

body.text: Do not worry about feeling ashamed. These calls are built to work on people who love their families, which is not a weakness.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a next step, and speed is the thing that helps.

items: You sent money an hour ago: call the bank now, since early reports sometimes stop the transfer.
You gave account details but sent nothing: watch the account and change the password.
The caller is still calling: do not argue. Block the number and write down what was said.
A relative's voice appears in a voice note: call them on their number to confirm.
You are unsure whether a call was real: ask the family question, and treat silence as a no.
Your number was used in the same scam: warn your contacts, since they will be targeted next.

body.text: Practice
Agree the family question today, while nothing is happening.

items: Choose a question whose answer is not on social media.
Agree it with two family members and write it down.
Agree a second question, in case one is forgotten.
Save the bank's fraud number in your contacts.
Explain the rule to the person most likely to be called.

body.text: You can now hear a familiar voice and still check it. In the next lesson you will clear out the apps, subscriptions, and accounts you no longer use.

excerpt: A yearly pass over your phone and accounts: uninstalling what you never open, cancelling forgotten subscriptions, and closing old accounts properly.

body.text: This lesson is a yearly clean-up: removing apps you never open, cancelling subscriptions you forgot, closing old accounts, and clearing files that take up space. An hour once a year keeps the phone faster and the bank balance honest.
Digital clutter is quiet. It costs storage, battery, and sometimes money every month, and nobody notices until the storage warning appears.
Before you start

items: The phone, charged, on wifi.
A bank statement for the last three months.
About an hour, and a second session for anything unfinished.

body.text: Remove the apps you do not open

items: Open the app list and sort by last used, if the phone allows it.
Uninstall anything you have not opened in three months.
Keep the ones you need rarely but truly need, such as a bank app.
Check the app sizes first, since one large game can free more than twenty small ones.
Revoke permissions for apps you keep but rarely use.
Download the file of photos before uninstalling anything that stores them.

body.text: You will see the storage figure at the top of the settings screen drop as each app is removed, and the home screen lose an icon. The freeing is visible within seconds.

body.alt: A phone showing an uninstall confirmation for a seldom-used app.
body.caption: Uninstalling removes the app and its data from the phone. Accounts on the service stay open until you close them separately.

body.text: It looks like uninstalling an app cancels the subscription. It removes the app from the phone, and the monthly charge continues until you cancel it in the store.
Find the subscriptions

items: On Android, open the Play Store, then Payments and subscriptions.
On an iPhone, open Settings, then your name, then Subscriptions.
Read each entry and its renewal date.
Cancel anything you have not used in two months.
Cancel in the store rather than in the app, which is where the charge begins.
Read the bank statement for the last three months and match each repeat charge.

body.text: The subscription list will show the price and the next billing date beside each service, which is often the first time you see the total. Add them up before deciding what stays.

body.alt: A phone subscription screen listing services with prices and renewal dates.
body.caption: Every repeat charge in one list. Cancelling here stops the payment, which uninstalling never does.

body.text: Close the accounts you have left

items: List the accounts you opened and no longer use, starting with shopping sites.
Search the service's help pages for how to delete the account, since it is often buried.
Download anything you need before deleting, such as receipts or photos.
Delete rather than deactivate, unless you may return.
Remove the app afterwards, so the account does not come back with it.
Keep a short list of accounts you closed and the date, for your own records.

body.text: None of this is urgent, and doing it all in one evening is a mistake. One category a month finishes the whole job by the end of the year.
Do not worry about losing something you might need. Keep the accounts you use once a year, and close only the ones you had forgotten existed.
If it goes wrong
Every case here has a route back, and none of them is permanent on the same day.

items: You cancelled the wrong subscription: resubscribe, which takes two minutes.
An app you removed held your photos: check the service's website before panicking.
The charge continues after cancelling: check the store's confirmation email, then call the provider.
You deleted an account by mistake: start a new one, and note the loss for next year.
The bank statement has a charge you cannot identify: call the bank rather than ignoring it.
The phone is slower after the clean-up: restart it, which clears the temporary files.

body.text: Practice
One category today, and put the rest in the calendar.

items: Uninstall three apps you have not opened this month.
Open the subscription list and read every price.
Cancel one subscription you do not use.
Note one account to close next month.
Write the date in the calendar, one year from today.

body.text: You can now keep a phone tidy and a budget honest. In the next lesson you will teach somebody else, which is the fastest way to be sure you know it.

excerpt: How to teach a nervous beginner without taking the mouse from them, the order to teach things in, and why the person who teaches learns most.

body.text: This lesson teaches you to teach somebody else: a parent, a shop assistant, a younger sibling. You will learn the order to teach things in, how to sit beside rather than take over, and how to leave them able to do it alone.
Teaching is a separate skill from doing. A person who grabs the mouse and finishes the task has done the work and taught nothing, which is why patience matters more than knowledge.
Before you start

items: One person who has asked for help.
Twenty minutes without interruption.
A task they actually need: sending a photo, checking a balance, printing a page.

body.text: Start with the task, not the theory

items: Ask what they want to do today, in their own words.
Choose one task only, even if they list five.
Show the whole task once at normal speed, while they watch.
Then do it again slowly, saying each step out loud.
Then let them do it while you stay silent.
Finish when the task is done, not when the topic is exhausted.

body.text: You will see their hand hover over the mouse before they click, which is the moment to wait. Every extra second of waiting is a step they will remember.

body.alt: Two people at a computer, one watching while the other uses the mouse.
body.caption: Sit at the side, not in front. The hand on the mouse should be theirs for most of the session.

body.text: It looks like explaining faster covers more ground. A learner who does one task alone has learned more than one who watched five tasks being done for them.
Rules that keep it kind

items: Do not take the mouse or the phone from their hand, even to save a minute.
Say the step, then wait, rather than doing it as you speak.
Accept a slower method if it works for them.
Repeat the same task in the next session, since repetition is the whole method.
Never say the word simple, which turns a struggle into a personal failure.
Praise the step they got right rather than the speed.

body.text: None of this needs teaching materials. One task, done three times, on their own device, is the entire curriculum for a week.

A short list of steps will appear on the paper in the learner's own words, often in a different order from the menu. You will see which step they remember and which one they skip, and the skipped one is tomorrow's lesson.

body.alt: A small group learning around one laptop in a room.
body.caption: One laptop and three learners works if each of them takes a turn with the mouse. Watching is not practising.

body.text: Write the steps down together

items: After the task, ask them to say the steps while you write.
Use their words, not the menu's words, where the two differ.
Draw the screen if a drawing is clearer than a sentence.
Keep the paper beside the device, where it will be used.
Add the step they forgot, without comment.
Photograph the paper, so it survives being lost.

body.text: Do not worry about the notes looking untidy. Notes in the learner's own words are the ones they will read, and neat notes in your words are the ones they will ignore.
If it goes wrong
Every case here is about pace or patience, and both can be adjusted.

items: They forget the steps within a day: repeat the task tomorrow, which is normal rather than failure.
They ask you to do it: agree to do it once, then ask them to repeat it.
They are embarrassed: name something you found hard to learn, which lowers the room.
They learn a different way that works: leave it alone, since the goal is the task.
You lose patience: stop the session, and continue tomorrow rather than pressing on.
They cannot read the screen: make the text larger, which is a separate lesson.

body.text: Practice
Teach one task this week, from start to finish, without touching the mouse.

items: Choose one person and one task.
Show it once, then slowly, then not at all.
Keep your hands away from the mouse.
Write the steps in their words.
Ask them to do it alone tomorrow and tell you how it went.

body.text: You can now pass on what you know, which is how a household stops needing to ask. In the next lesson you will look at the work a cybersecurity analyst actually does.
